lines.para: In January 1942, the Japanese round up Hong Kong’s “enemy” civilians on the Stanley peninsula, in the south of the island: about 2,800 people, mostly British, but also Americans, Dutch and Canadians. Families included.
The camp occupies the buildings of a college and the staff quarters of the neighbouring prison. Several families are crammed into a single room.
The ration, mostly rice, is not enough. Beriberi and malnutrition set in. People garden, barter, buy on the black market from the guards.
Even so, the internees organise classes, concerts and plays.
In January 1945, an American plane mistakenly bombs a building in the camp and kills fourteen internees.
The camp is not liberated until August 1945, after Japan’s surrender.
